questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given the Value of Their Dot Product
questions.problem: Given that $c\cdot d=11$, find the angle between $c=⟨2t,1⟩$ and $d=⟨2,3⟩.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
First, since $c\cdot d=11$, we can solve for $t$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot d & =11 \\ 2t\cdot 2+1\cdot 3 & =11 \\ 4t+3 & =11 \\ 4t & =8 \\ t & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =⟨2(2),1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $c$ and $d$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{c\cdot d}{|\,c\,||\,d\,|} \\  & =\frac{{c}_{x}{d}_{x}+{c}_{y}{d}_{y}}{\sqrt{{c}_{x}^{2}+{c}_{y}^{2}}\sqrt{{d}_{x}^{2}+{d}_{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{17}\cdot \sqrt{13}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{221}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{11}{\sqrt{221}})≈{42.27}^{∘}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given Three Points
questions.problem: Find $∠BAC$ given the points $A(2,1,-1)$, $B(3,-2,2)$, and $C(-1,-2,1).$ Round your answer to the nearest degree.
questions.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $A$, $B$, $C$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}a=⟨2,1,-1⟩,\,b=⟨3,-2,2⟩,\,c=⟨-1,-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle $△ABC$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠BAC=\theta .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14046481/assets/285b8343208079181ac6036cf9ca16abc974d59b9262878ed40c0da9af5683d0.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =⟨3,-2,2⟩-⟨2,1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-3,3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =⟨-1,-2,1⟩-⟨2,1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,-3,2⟩\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot \overset{\to }{AC}}{|\overset{\to }{AB}||\overset{\to }{AC}|} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (-3)+(-3)\cdot (-3)+3\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{3}^{2}}\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{19}\cdot \sqrt{22}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{418}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{12}{\sqrt{418}})≈{54}^{∘}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given Three Points
questions.worked_solution:
Note that the position vectors of the points $P$, $Q$, $R$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}p=⟨1,5,-1⟩,\,q=⟨5,1,1⟩,\,r=⟨2,5,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The $△PQR$ is shown (schematically) in the diagram below, where we denote $∠QPR=\theta .$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14046481/assets/3003f0cb329a8f8ef9bc315c70df4773ac1f0c54843dea1208c68bd0f6227bd1.png)

First, we find the components of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to }{PR}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =q-p \\  & =⟨5,1,1⟩-⟨1,5,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-4,2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{PR} & =r-p \\  & =⟨2,5,0⟩-⟨1,5,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to }{PR}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot \overset{\to }{PR}}{|\overset{\to }{PQ}||\overset{\to }{PR}|} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 1+(-4)\cdot 0+2\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{36}\cdot \sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})={45}^{∘}.
$$

questions.problem: Given that $p\cdot q=11$, find the angle between $p=⟨t,t-1⟩$ and $q=⟨-4,-1⟩.$ Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.
questions.worked_solution:
First, since $p\cdot q=11$, we can solve for $t$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & =11 \\ t\cdot (-4)+(t-1)\cdot (-1) & =11 \\ -4t-t+1 & =11 \\ -5t & =10 \\ t & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨(-2),(-2)-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $p$ and $q$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{p\cdot q}{|\,p\,||\,q\,|} \\  & =\frac{{p}_{x}{q}_{x}+{p}_{y}{q}_{y}}{\sqrt{{p}_{x}^{2}+{p}_{y}^{2}}\sqrt{{q}_{x}^{2}+{q}_{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-3)^{2}}\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{13}\cdot \sqrt{17}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{221}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{11}{\sqrt{221}})≈{42.3}^{∘}.
$$

questions.problem: Given that $a\cdot b=-9$, find the angle between $a=⟨-2t,3t⟩$ and $b=⟨3,1⟩.$ Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.
questions.worked_solution:
First, since $a\cdot b=-9$, we can solve for $t$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =-9 \\ -2t\cdot 3+3t\cdot 1 & =-9 \\ -6t+3t & =-9 \\ -3t & =-9 \\ t & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =⟨-2(3),\,3(3)⟩ \\  & =⟨-6,9⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the cosine of the angle between $a$ and $b$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,||\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}}\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-9}{\sqrt{(-6)^{2}+{9}^{2}}\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =-\frac{9}{\sqrt{117}\cdot \sqrt{10}} \\  & =-\frac{9}{3\sqrt{13}\cdot \sqrt{10}} \\  & =-\frac{3}{\sqrt{130}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-\frac{3}{\sqrt{130}})≈{105.3}^{∘}.
$$
